explanation: Fires on the token where a second item in a parallel list or repeated structure starts, after a near-copy of the same pattern just appeared: android[:]layout_height after layout_width, flc_hi after flc_lo, dest2 after dest1, -moz- after -webkit-, a second 'print'/'expected'. Also fires more weakly on some list continuations in prose. The repetition in the preceding context matters more than the token itself.

Fires on words about a person's body, self or identity, usually in contexts of violence, transformation or personal information: 'severed heads', 'bludgeoned to death', 'transforming into', 'photos of themselves/myself', 'robot form', 'Personal (identifiable) information', 'identity theft', 'Category:1977 births'. Looks like a loose 'the self/person as an object (killed, changed, pictured, identified)' concept.

Fires on a contrastive or modifying word partway through a phrase, often 'external', 'foreign', 'not', 'reverse', 'backwards', 'from' (as in 'immigrant from'), 'but', 'since'. Many hits are on 'external'/'External links' and on negation or contrast words ('not the expulsion', 'not even released'); the rest look heterogeneous.

Fires on vague discourse or anaphoric words in informal English prose that point back to earlier context or link clauses: 'such', 'it', 'why', 'reason(s)', 'stuff', 'issue', 'as a result', 'Plus', 'Again', 'Various', 'all'. The token must be one of these general reference or connective words; content words fire weakly or not at all.

Fires on punctuation and operator tokens inside code and URLs that join a key or name to its value or argument: '=' in URL query strings (?id=, ?user=), [' in PHP array keys, ':' / ':@"' in Objective-C message arguments, '():', '.php', '.min', '\frac' in LaTeX. Plain prose fires only weakly.

Fires inside scientific or technical text (medicine, physics, chemistry) on a field or domain word, or the 'in/and' just before one ('fields in condensed matter', 'areas of medical physics', 'physics and engineering', 'biological and synthetic'). It also fires on the first subword of rare multi-token names or terms ('epid'ural, 'Tur'boprops/Turán, 'Lov'ins, 'flav'iviruses). Two jobs: academic-domain context and the start of split proper or technical names.

Fires on the end of a clause or sentence, and on word-final pieces or particles, in non-English text (German, Danish, Turkish, Japanese, Russian, Vietnamese) and on sentence-ending periods in scientific abstracts. Strongest for verb endings and clause-final punctuation in foreign languages; English prose periods outside abstracts fire weakly.

Mixed: fires on '.android' in 'http://schemas.android.com', on middle digits of multi-digit numbers in math or data text, on 'Warp'/'WARP', and on physical-science nouns ('field of fire', 'pressure', 'standing wave', 'sand', 'spacesuit', 'spectrometer'). No shared concept is obvious.

Fires on the space or punctuation inside fixed formulaic templates: the space before the year in dates ('29 October 2016', 'Mon, 02 Mar 2015'), the ':' in '(Ancient Greek: ...)', 'free of charge' in MIT licences, '== null' in Java, 'Grade Point'. The cue is a highly predictable stock pattern; the token is the predictable next piece.

Fires on the head noun of a technical compound term, completing a domain-specific noun phrase: 'co-operative', 'stent', 'antigen', 'Antenna', 'RAT', 'fuel cell', 'BSD-style license', 'Material', 'Matchers', 'Strain'. Strongest when the noun is a concrete technical object or entity named right after its modifier.

Hard to unify. It fires on surname pieces in legal 'Before X, Y, Z' judge lists (MARTIN, ELLIOTT), on 'of' in 'of all the...' and 'the Forest Gump of', on 'am' in 'What am I doing wrong', on separators closing items in lists of test names or citations, and on words like 'problems', 'hardest', 'WHY'. No single trigger is evident.

Fires on the term defined inside a parenthetical quoted short-form definition, '(the "License")' in software licence headers and '("GE")', '("Cooley")', '"Danny"' in legal or biographical text. Weaker on acronyms defined in parentheses in scientific text ('(BM)', '(CNS)'). The quote-in-parenthesis defining context is what matters.

Fires on short function words and word pieces in Romance-language text (Spanish, French, Portuguese, Romanian): 'de', 'à', 'a', 'no', 'ou', 'án'. More weakly it fires on a capital letter 'A'/'G' starting a name or acronym in English ('A-League', 'GABA'). Mainly: Romance-language function tokens.

Fires on a token that begins a predictable continuation in a fixed or formulaic phrase: 'the [family]' in 'is a moth of the family X', 'The' in titles ('The Entertainer', 'The Muppets'), 'under' in 'licenses this file to You under', 'TWENTY-' in chapter lists. Many contexts are mixed; the taxonomy 'family' pattern is the clearest.

Fires on the word naming the form or format something takes after 'in', especially 'binary' in BSD licence text ('in source and binary forms', 'Redistributions in binary form'). Also 'in the form of', 'in game format', 'in paperback', 'in its final form', 'in any form'. The 'in ___ form/format' context is key.

Fires mostly in HTML, XML and code on the attribute or keyword that starts the next element after a tag or a repeated sibling line: ' class' in '<li class', ' src' in '<script type=... src', ' android' in an XML attribute, ' struct' in a parameter list, '<option'. Also a few unrelated prose hits ('Working over', 'GOT TIME'). Main job: an attribute or keyword in repetitive markup.

Fires on mid-sentence words, often verbs or negation ('sont', 'niet', 'estar', 'se', 'en'), in non-English European prose (French, Dutch, Portuguese). It also fires on the first piece of rare split proper names in English ('Nighthawks', 'Remigius', 'FREQUENCY', 'Oslo', 'National Register'). Two jobs: foreign-language function words and fragments of uncommon names.

Fires on clinical or biomedical description tokens, especially symptoms and findings in case reports ('weakness of right side', 'paralysis', 'pain', 'scans revealed a', 'volume', '99mTc'). Strongest on deficit or symptom nouns after a clinical presentation; scattered weak hits in code or other text.

Fires where a complement or embedded clause opens: 'import (' in Go source, and in prose the complementizer after verbs of asking, deciding or saying ('decide whether', 'clarify whether', 'suggesting that', 'argues that', 'check if'). Two related jobs: Go import blocks and the start of complement clauses.

Fires on the middle or later pieces of rare multi-token words, mostly drug, chemical and biomedical names ('methot[rex]ate', 'lumefantr[ine]', 'interleuk[in]', 'ranibiz[um]ab', 'dehydrogen[ase]'), and also on tails of other rare words or names ('Sh[h]', 'Ph[ew]', 'Tin[jar]'). It is predicting how a familiar long word finishes.

Fires on the second part of common fixed bigrams and set expressions: '$50 per share', '(Reuters)', 'critically ill', 'American League', '<ul id', 'ANOVA', ' (@' in tweet attributions, 'type 1 diabetes'. The token is a highly predictable completion of a stock phrase or markup idiom.
